data.text:
Captain Dixie Kiefer in battle dress on the command bridge of USS Ticonderoga during the launching of aircraft against Luzon, Philippines, Nov 6, 1944. 

Kiefer was widely regarded as one of the most battered yet indefatigable officers in the Navy: he had broken his left ankle and split his kneecap playing football as a youth, and later suffered a smashed elbow when a fellow pilot buzzed him in a seaplane and clipped his arm with a float. The crew of Ticonderoga quipped that “he’s got so much metal in him the ship’s compass follows him when he walks across the deck.”

Dixie Kiefer (April 5, 1896 – November 11, 1945) was a senior officer in the United States Navy who served with distinction during both World War I and World War II. Born in Blackfoot, Idaho, and later raised in Lincoln, Nebraska (where he graduated from Lincoln High School), Kiefer entered the United States Naval Academy in 1915 and was commissioned in June 1918. 

Following his commissioning, his first assignment was aboard USS Corona, an anti-submarine patrol vessel operating in European waters near the end of World War I. 

In the 1920s, Kiefer became a naval aviator: on November 11, 1924, flying a Vought UO-1 catapult-launched from USS California in San Diego harbor, he made the first ever night take-off from a warship, using only the ship’s searchlights for illumination. 

By World War II, Kiefer had risen to commander and served as Executive Officer of the aircraft carrier USS Yorktown (CV 5) during the Battles of Coral Sea and Midway, where his leadership and high morale-building earned him the Distinguished Service Medal and the Navy Cross respectively. 

During the sinking of Yorktown at Midway, he fractured his right leg and ankle while leaping from the ship. 

After recovering from his injuries, Kiefer was promoted to captain and given command of the new carrier USS Ticonderoga (CV 14), commissioned May 8, 1944 at the Norfolk Navy Yard. 

Known for his hands-on leadership and popularity with the crew, he reportedly used a bullhorn several times a day to expedite flight deck operations and offered shore leave and quality meals to bolster crew morale. 

On January 21, 1945, while operating in the Pacific, Ticonderoga was struck by two Japanese kamikaze attackers. The first hit set the hangar deck ablaze with flaming gasoline and aircraft; Kiefer ordered the flooding of a port-side compartment to give the ship a 10-degree list, causing the burning gasoline to slide overboard—a tactic not previously employed—and moved the ship upwind of the wreckage. 

The second strike wounded him (65 shrapnel injuries) and broke his arm; he remained on the bridge in command for eleven hours until all other injured personnel were stabilized. 

While still recovering from these severe injuries, Kiefer was made an honorary commodore in a ceremony at Rockefeller Center and later commanded Naval Air Station Quonset in Rhode Island. 

Sadly, on November 11, 1945, at the age of 49, he died in the crash of his Navy transport plane while returning from Caldwell, New Jersey to Quonset, New York—his arm still in a cast. 

Kiefer was interred at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

data.text: While not yet formally called, #UwanPH, tropical storm #FungWong remains forecasted to bring intense rainfall to most of Luzon and parts south in the Philippines beginning on Sunday and it is forecast to make landfall as a Super Typhoon. Prepare now. This could bring life threatening flooding and overwhelm existing flood control measures in addition to gale force winds across much of central and northern Luzon.
